note: Finds GPT-4 guesses masked MMLU options 57 percent of the time, direct evidence of test set exposure in a closed model.
title: Investigating Data Contamination in Modern Benchmarks for Large Language Models
explain_beginner: If a powerful AI model like GPT-4 was accidentally trained on internet text that includes a benchmark test's answer key, it would score better on that test without actually being smarter, and the trick would be nearly invisible from the outside since nobody outside the company can see what data went into training it. Deng and coauthors designed a clever way to test for exactly this without needing access to that private training data, they took multiple choice questions from a popular test, MMLU, hid the correct answer option, and asked models to guess what the missing option probably was, based purely on the surrounding question text. A model that has never seen the test before should guess correctly only about as often as chance allows, but the researchers found GPT-4 correctly guessed the exact hidden answer more than half the time, a result far above what chance alone would produce, and consistent with the test questions having appeared in its training data. This gives real evidence for a suspicion many researchers already had, that closed, undisclosed training data can make benchmark comparisons between AI models unreliable in ways nobody outside the company that built the model can fully verify.
explain_business: The direct implication for any organization comparing AI models using published benchmark scores is that even the most capable closed, proprietary models, the study's headline finding involves GPT-4 specifically, can show behavior consistent with having memorized parts of a widely used test, MMLU, that they are then scored against, and because that training data is not disclosed, no outside party can simply check for this the way you could with an open source model's training set. Practically, this means benchmark comparisons involving closed commercial models deserve added skepticism specifically when the benchmark in question is old and widely circulated online, like MMLU, since models trained on huge internet scrapes had ample opportunity to encounter it directly or indirectly during training. Organizations making high stakes model selection decisions should weight benchmark performance on demonstrably contamination resistant or private evaluation sets more heavily than a public, long available benchmark, and treat published scores on well known benchmarks like MMLU as an upper bound on demonstrated ability rather than a precise measurement of it.
explain_practitioner: The authors propose two contamination detection methods that do not require access to a model's training data, a retrieval based method that checks for overlap between benchmark text and publicly crawlable web content the model may have trained on, and Testset Slot Guessing (TS-Guessing), which masks an answer option in a multiple choice question, or an unlikely word in an open text passage, and measures whether the model can correctly fill in the masked content well above chance, a signal of prior memorized exposure rather than reasoning. Applying TS-Guessing to MMLU with masked answer options, they measured a 52 percent exact match rate for ChatGPT and 57 percent for GPT-4, both far exceeding the baseline guess rate expected from reasoning alone. They also found that adding metadata typically associated with a benchmark's original source materially improved model performance on TruthfulQA, a second, independent signal consistent with memorized exposure to that benchmark's specific formatting rather than the underlying question itself. The method's inherent limitation is that it detects a strong correlate of contamination, unexpectedly accurate guessing of masked content, rather than directly proving training data inclusion, since it cannot inspect the training corpus itself.
